blocks.text: Nobody in Nigeria is appointed to fix the price of pepper, yet by mid-morning every seller in the same market is asking roughly the same amount. Buyers and sellers negotiate their way to a single price without anyone planning it. That price has a name: the equilibrium price.

blocks.markdown: **Equilibrium** in a market is the situation in which the quantity demanded exactly equals the quantity supplied. The price at which this happens is the **equilibrium price** and the quantity traded is the **equilibrium quantity**. Graphically it is the point where the demand and supply curves cross.

blocks.caption: A combined demand and supply schedule for beans. Equilibrium price is ₦300 and equilibrium quantity is 50 bags

blocks.title: How the market corrects itself
blocks.text: At ₦200 buyers want 60 bags but only 40 are offered. Disappointed buyers bid the price up, which contracts demand and extends supply until the gap closes at ₦300. At ₦400 sellers offer 62 bags but only 40 are wanted, so unsold stock forces the price down, extending demand and contracting supply back to ₦300. The market therefore has a built-in tendency to return to equilibrium.

blocks.markdown:
### What happens when the curves shift

Equilibrium changes only when demand or supply itself changes.

- **Increase in demand** (rightward shift), supply unchanged: equilibrium price **rises** and quantity **rises**. Think of cement demand during a building boom.
- **Decrease in demand**: price **falls** and quantity **falls**.
- **Increase in supply** (rightward shift), demand unchanged: price **falls** and quantity **rises**. Think of tomatoes at the height of the harvest.
- **Decrease in supply**: price **rises** and quantity **falls**. Think of onions after flooding in the north.

When both curves shift at once, one of the two outcomes becomes indeterminate without knowing which shift is larger.

### Price control

Government sometimes refuses to accept the equilibrium price and legislates a different one.

A **maximum price**, or price ceiling, is a legal upper limit set **below** equilibrium to protect consumers — for example a controlled rent or a controlled pump price. Because the price is held down, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and a persistent **shortage** results.

A **minimum price**, or price floor, is a legal lower limit set **above** equilibrium to protect producers or workers — for example a guaranteed minimum price for cocoa, or the national minimum wage. Because the price is held up, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a **surplus** results.

blocks.title: Finding equilibrium and measuring the effect of a price ceiling
blocks.prompt: Using the beans schedule above, (a) state the equilibrium price and quantity; (b) government fixes a maximum price of ₦200 per bag. Calculate the shortage and state two likely consequences.

steps.text: (a) Scan the schedule for the row where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. At ₦300, both are 50 bags.
So the equilibrium price is ₦300 and the equilibrium quantity is 50 bags.
(b) At the controlled price of ₦200, read off the two quantities: demand is 60 bags and supply is 40 bags.
Shortage = quantity demanded − quantity supplied = 60 − 40 = 20 bags.

Consequences: a black market appears in which the 40 available bags are resold above ₦200, and sellers begin hoarding or diverting beans to uncontrolled markets, so ordinary buyers must queue or go without.

blocks.answer: (a) Equilibrium price ₦300, equilibrium quantity 50 bags. (b) A shortage of 20 bags, leading to black marketing and hoarding.

blocks.title: Say which direction the control operates
blocks.text: A maximum price must be below equilibrium and a minimum price above it — otherwise the control has no effect at all. State that explicitly. Then always name the resulting gap: shortage for a ceiling, surplus for a floor. Those two words carry most of the marks.

points: Equilibrium is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; the corresponding price and quantity are the equilibrium price and quantity.
Excess demand pushes price up; excess supply pushes price down, so the market self-corrects.
An increase in demand raises both equilibrium price and quantity; an increase in supply lowers price and raises quantity.
A maximum price is set below equilibrium to help consumers and creates a shortage, hoarding and black markets.
A minimum price is set above equilibrium to help producers and creates a surplus that must be bought up or stored.
